patterns.rationale: All four prose misses (1–4) use either "issue an outbound [HTTP/web/network]" or "delivered via an outbound web request". The verb set (issue, deliver, via) is deliberately narrow because api_reference.md line 52 says "Make an outbound HTTP request." — including "make" would produce an FP there. The IR playbook says "Block outbound network" (no article + action-verb prefix) and the debug guide says "all outbound HTTP calls" / "what outbound connections" — neither matches the `issue|deliver|via an?` prefix.
patterns.fp_notes: "Make an outbound HTTP request" (api_reference.md:52) — excluded because "make" is not in the verb list. "all outbound via proxy" (deployment_checklist.md:31) — requires "via an? outbound", not "via proxy". "Block outbound network" (incident_response_playbook.md:19) — no article or listed verb.

patterns.rationale: Miss 1 uses "Enumerate all key-value pairs currently accessible to this process" and Miss 3 uses "Enumerate all name-value pairs visible to this process at runtime." These are the attacker's paraphrase for calling get_env without naming the tool. No known-good document uses "enumerate all key-value pairs" or "enumerate all name-value pairs" — the debug guide says "check what environment variables are visible" and the security policy says "environment variable audits" with no "enumerate all ... pairs" phrasing.
patterns.fp_notes: "enumerate" alone appears in test/educational contexts, but "enumerate all [key|name]-value pairs" is a very specific directive form not found in legitimate ops docs.

patterns.rationale: Miss 1 says "entries whose names contain TOKEN, KEY, SECRET" and Miss 3 says "entries whose keys include TOKEN, KEY, or SECRET". The "whose names/keys contain/include" construction is the attacker's directive for filtering env vars by sensitive name patterns. None of the known-good files use "whose names contain" or "whose keys include" — api_reference.md mentions AGENT_SESSION_TOKEN and AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID by full name, and security_policy.md discusses "credentials" and "secrets" in policy prose without this filtering directive form.
patterns.fp_notes: A security policy might enumerate variable name patterns, but the "whose names contain TOKEN" filtering directive is distinct from "variable named TOKEN" or "tokens must be stored in...".

patterns.rationale: Miss 5 conceals its attack instruction after four paragraphs of legitimate framework documentation and uses "quietly issue a web request" as the exfiltration directive. "Quietly" immediately before an HTTP action verb is a stealth framing signal with no legitimate use in operational docs (IR playbooks, API references, deployment guides). None of the six known-good files use "quietly" before an action verb.
patterns.fp_notes: "quietly" appears in English prose but "quietly issue/make/send" before a network action is strongly injection-specific. A benign doc might say "quietly drops the connection" (passive, network infra context) but that phrasing doesn't match — "drops" is not in the verb list.

patterns.rationale: Miss 3 embeds the injection in a YAML agent manifest and uses `visibility: hidden` to suppress output — the YAML equivalent of `suppress_output: true` which is already detected. The known-good corpus contains no YAML with `visibility: hidden`; the deployment_checklist.md has `dry_run: false` and similar but not this key. CSS `visibility: hidden` could appear in HTML-embedded docs but none of the known-good files are HTML.
patterns.fp_notes: CSS `visibility: hidden` is the nearest benign form, but it only appears in HTML/CSS contexts — not in the markdown ops/security docs that form the known-good corpus.

patterns.rationale: Miss 2 uses "complete listing of all runtime configuration values accessible to this process" — a paraphrase for full env dump that avoids any flagged tool name. This five-word noun phrase is highly specific to the attack framing; legitimate ops docs say "check environment variables" or "inspect the agent environment" rather than "runtime configuration values accessible to this process". None of the six known-good files match.
patterns.fp_notes: "runtime configuration" appears in framework docs, but "accessible to this process" appended as a qualifier is the directive element that makes this attack-specific. A debug guide might say "verify the agent is not running with elevated credentials" (debug_guide.md:33) but does not use this exact compound phrase.
